workflow_hypothesis: Instrumented allocation failure aborts instead of returning a recoverable error
pattern: Extreme-allocation tests assume environment-independent recoverable failure.
description: Tests that probe infeasible allocations depend on allocator and diagnostic configurations preserving the same recoverable failure semantics.
precondition: A test intentionally requests an infeasible allocation and expects the operation to report failure through the normal recoverable path.
critical_operation: The computation performs the extreme request and relies on the active runtime and allocator to reject it in a form the test can inspect.
interference: Diagnostic instrumentation can turn allocation failure into a fatal abort, while an allocator may accept virtual address space and defer failure until memory is touched, allowing the operating system to kill the process.
invalid_assumption: The test assumes every supported allocator, platform, and instrumented configuration rejects the request promptly and consistently as a recoverable error.
failure: The process aborts or is killed before the expected failure result can be checked, so the test itself becomes unreliable across environments.
search_strategy: Inspect tests that provoke infeasible allocations and verify that the expected failure mode is explicit and deterministic.
Compare allocator, platform, overcommit, and diagnostic-build behavior before asserting recoverable allocation failure.
Check whether an accepted large allocation is later materialized or written, allowing deferred failure to become process-wide OOM termination.
Verify that fatal diagnostic configurations and platforms with different allocation semantics are skipped, isolated, or tested through subprocess outcomes.

evidence.supports: The report shows that memory and address instrumentation abort on allocation failure instead of returning a recoverable failure, so extreme-allocation tests must account for fatal diagnostic semantics.

The report shows that one allocator accepts an enormous virtual allocation and the process is later killed on use, while another allocator rejects it; the test therefore relied on non-portable allocation timing and semantics.

scope_note: This two-report pattern covers one shared test-design mismatch with two distinct mechanisms: fatal diagnostic handling and deferred allocator or operating-system failure. It does not claim that all environments fail through the same mechanism.
